articles.author: Null String
articles.description:
Remember when the invigilator shouted "pens down!"? I turned that into a quiz app.


That exact moment — pens hitting the desk at once, everyone caught mid-thought — is the whole idea behind PenDown, a live quiz app I just built and shipped.
🔗 Try it: https://pendown.live
Someone hosts a quiz (or just launches the built-in demo — takes 5 seconds)
Everyone else joins from their phone with a 6-character code — no signup, no app to install
Questions come in live with a countdown
When time's up, every screen gets stamped: PEN DOWN!

Live leaderboard after every question, final results at the end
It's built for the exact moment you'd actually use it — a college quiz night, a team icebreaker, a family group chat challenge, killing time with friends.
I want strangers to break it before real users do. Friends are too nice when they test things. So:
Grab a friend, coworker, or literally anyone in a group chat and play a round together (it's way more fun with 2+ people)
Try the demo quiz if you just want to poke around solo
Tell me what felt off, slow, confusing, or just didn't land
Genuinely curious whether the nostalgia hook lands for people who didn't grow up with the same "pens down" moment, too — would love to hear if this feels universal or very specifically an Indian-exam-hall thing.
https://pendown.live — go make some noise.
articles.title: I built PenDown — a live quiz app named after 'pens down!' Come break it

articles.author: Dave Kurian
articles.description:
The coding agents got good at layout. Ask Cursor, Claude Code, or Lovable for a pricing card and you get a recognisable, mostly-correct row of features with a button on the bottom — in about three seconds. The thing they're not good at is the part underneath: which blue, how much spacing, which grey for borders, what radius pairs with what shadow. They pick from an infinite palette and they pick badly.
A constrained token set is the cheapest, most reliable guardrail you can put in front of that. The surprise isn't that tokens help. The surprise is how aggressively they help the agent — not the human.
Here's what an unconstrained agent produces for "build me a pricing page" in a fresh project, most of the time:

articles.author: Michael
articles.description:
The built‑in gcrecover service in GBase 8a handles the recovery of data synchronization events. With the gcadmin recover command, DBAs can dynamically control recovery behavior — pausing or resuming tasks, and setting per‑VC priority for specific event types — without restarting any services. This article walks through the available subcommands with practical examples and log interpretation.
Run gcadmin --help and look for the recover section to confirm your version supports this feature. The available operations are:
pause: Stop scheduling new recovery tasks; in‑flight tasks continue to completion.
continue: Resume normal recovery scheduling.
highpriority vc_name [event_type]: Assign priority to a specific VC. The optional event_type can be ddlevent, dmlevent, or dmlstorage.
show status: …
